newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Protesters' battles with Balkan rulers deadlocked.
newsitem.headline: Protesters' battles with Balkan rulers deadlocked.

text.p: Bitter struggles between mass protest movements and governments in Bulgaria and Serbia remained deadlocked on Friday and financial scandals threatened to ignite a popular uprising in another Balkan state, Albania.

Demoralised populations in a corner of ex-communist eastern Europe which has failed dismally to make a smooth switch to democracy and capitalism are being driven on to the streets by different grievances but their slogans and methods are similar.

Thousands marched in Sofia for a 12th day and one-hour strikes were held nationwide to demand early elections from a Socialist government whose economic bungling is blamed for annual inflation running at a rate of 300 percent and the descent of millions of citizens into poverty.
The renamed ruling party of the old communist state won a freely held general election in 1994 largely because Bulgarians imagined them to be more competent than their opponents.

Demonstrators now portray them as both corrupt and inept, after little reform of the crumbling, mostly state-run economy. Protesting students appealed on Friday for an investigation into powerful business groups and their links with politicians.
One opinion poll gave the Socialists just eight percent support, and the government is holding out to delay until late 1997 elections likely to sweep them from power if held sooner.

On Friday they stuck to their insistence on forming a new cabinet but said talks with the opposition Union of Democratic Forces could resume when president-elect Petar Stoyanov -- a member of the opposition -- is sworn in on Sunday.

Bulgarians admit to following the example of the marathon protest movement in Serbia, where living standards are higher but discontent fierce with President Slobodan Milosevic's Socialists, another ex-communist ruling party, for alleged poll fraud in annulling November local election results.
The Belgrade opposition, after nine weeks of unrest, urged the West on Friday to step up pressure on Milosevic to respect his commitments to democracy in the 1995 Bosnian peace deal.
Bulgarians too are hoping for aid from the West, in the form of rescue cash from the IMF and World Bank who will only hand it over if tough monetary policies are introduced.

In Europe's poorest country, Albania, which unlike Bulgaria and Serbia is run by a rightist government, outrage among investors demanding money back from dubious get-rich-quick pyramid schemes threatened to stoke broader political unrest.

The opposition Socialists, centre-right Democratic Alliance and Social Democrats called on Friday for a protest in Tirana on Sunday, blaming the Democratic Party of President Sali Berisha for the collapse of three such schemes.
"The Socialist Party will support and lead the protection of people's interests, confronting the state with democratic action on a massive scale," a statement by the Socialists said.

Police remained stationed around Tirana to prevent a repeat of street clashes on Wednesday after a pyramid scheme run by a Gypsy woman called Sude collapsed. Protests spread on Thursday to the western city of Vlore and Shkoder in the north.

The schemes, which lured thousands of Albanians into selling everything they owned with promises of big returns on small outlays, mushroomed after the fall of communism in 1990. Four more have suspended payments to investors.
The government has ordered the seizure of 25.5 billion leks ($255 million) deposited by such schemes in state-owned banks.

But the opposition, which boycotted general elections last year claiming they were rigged by the Democrats, said the sequestration was a sign of the economic and institutional crisis within the state and repeated its call for new polls.
"The solution to the political and institutional crisis and economic collapse can be realised only through fresh elections," the Socialists' statement said.

In Greece, whose economic problems pale into insignificance beside those of its ex-communist neighbours, striking seamen said on Friday they would extend a five-day-old strike for better insurance, pension and tax benefits for four more days.

Police reported minor clashes in ports among passengers, lorry drivers and seamen. Aviation workers, pushing to keep tax breaks the government plans to end, also called for stoppages on Friday and Sunday. Officials said flights would be delayed.
